meta.titre: Argumentative Composition: arguing for or against a statement
meta.sous_theme: Planning and writing an essay that answers "Do you agree?"

source.epreuve_titre: GCE O/L English Language past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: In a quarter of Bamenda, two neighbours argue about whether children should help in the family shop after school. Each of them gives reasons, and each tries to show that the other has missed something. That is exactly what the Paper 2 composition asks of you when a statement is followed by "Do you agree?". Examiners are not looking for the "right" opinion. They are looking for a clear position, supported by reasons and examples, in well-organised and accurate English.

items: A paragraph deals with one main idea, and a new paragraph starts for each new idea.
A topic sentence is the sentence that states the main idea of a paragraph.
Linking words such as firstly, however and therefore join ideas and show how they relate.

sections.titre: How to write an argumentative essay
sections.contenu_markdown:
### What the question asks

A question such as "Pupils should do community work. Do you agree?" asks for your **opinion with reasons**. You may agree, disagree or partly agree, but you must choose one position and keep it from the introduction to the conclusion.

### Structure

| Part | What it contains |
|---|---|
| Introduction | One or two sentences of background, then a clear thesis: your answer to the question |
| Body paragraph 1 | Your strongest reason, explained and supported by an example |
| Body paragraph 2 | A second reason, explained and supported by an example |
| Opposing view | The best argument against you, then your reply to it (rebuttal) |
| Conclusion | Your position in new words and a final thought, with no new argument |

### Developing a paragraph

Use the pattern **point, explanation, example**. The point is the topic sentence. The explanation shows *why* it is true. The example makes it real and may come from daily life in Cameroon. A list of reasons without explanation scores badly, because it shows opinion but not argument.

### Useful linking words

| Job | Words |
|---|---|
| Adding a point | firstly, secondly, in addition, moreover |
| Giving a reason | because, since, this is because |
| Showing a result | therefore, as a result, consequently |
| Admitting the other side | it is true that, admittedly |
| Contrast | however, on the other hand, nevertheless |
| Concluding | in conclusion, to sum up |

### Style

Write in formal English: no text-message spelling, no slang, no abbreviations. Examiners judge the ideas (content), the clarity and organisation of the writing (expression) and the correctness of grammar, spelling and punctuation (accuracy).

variantes.quand_utiliser: When you have strong reasons for one side
variantes.contenu_markdown: State your position in the introduction. Give two or three developed reasons. Include one opposing argument and answer it, so the essay shows that you have considered the other side.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When both sides have real merit
variantes.contenu_markdown: Say clearly in the introduction what you accept and what you reject, for example "I agree, but only if ...". Make each body paragraph support that balanced position. Do not sit on the fence without any reasons.
Jot down your position, two or three reasons with an example for each, one opposing argument and your reply. Decide whether your strongest reason comes first or last, and then write the introduction.

sections.enonce_markdown:
Plan and write an answer to this question.

"Mobile phones should be allowed in secondary schools. Do you agree?"

etapes.action: Read the question and choose a position.
etapes.justification: The command is "Do you agree?", so the examiner wants an opinion. Decide before you write and keep to it.

etapes.action: List reasons, an opposing argument and a reply.
etapes.justification: A plan stops the essay from wandering. Each reason needs an example.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Reasons: (1) phones distract pupils; (2) phones make cheating easy. Opposing view: phones give access to information. Reply: this can be done outside school hours.

etapes.justification: Give brief background, then your thesis with the reasons you will develop.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Background about teenagers and phones, then "I do not agree, because ...".

etapes.action: Develop each body paragraph with point, explanation, example.
etapes.justification: This pattern turns a reason into an argument.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Paragraph 1: distraction, a message arrives, the pupil misses the lesson, tests suffer.

etapes.action: Admit and answer the other side, then conclude.
etapes.justification: A rebuttal shows mature thinking. The conclusion repeats the position and adds no new idea.
etapes.resultat_markdown: "It is true that ... However ..." then "In conclusion ...".

sections.conclusion_markdown:
A model answer:

Today almost every teenager dreams of owning a mobile phone, and some parents now think that phones should be allowed in classrooms. I do not agree, because phones distract pupils from their studies and make cheating easy.

First, phones distract pupils from their lessons. A pupil who hears a message arrive will want to read it at once, so he stops listening to the teacher. As a result, he misses important explanations and performs badly in tests.

Secondly, phones make cheating easy. During a test, a pupil can hide a phone under the desk and search for answers or receive them from a friend. Such a pupil learns nothing, and honest pupils are treated unfairly.

It is true that a phone can help a student to look for information or to call a parent in an emergency. However, these advantages can be enjoyed outside school hours, and the school office can contact parents when it is necessary.

In conclusion, although phones have some uses, the harm they do to learning and discipline is greater. For these reasons, I believe that secondary schools should not allow them.

items.erreur_markdown: The essay never states a position, or it begins with "Some people agree and others disagree" and stays there.
items.pourquoi_faux: The question asks what *you* think. An essay with no position cannot answer it.
items.correction_markdown: Give a clear thesis in the introduction, for example "I agree because ...", and keep to it.

items.erreur_markdown: A paragraph lists three reasons in one sentence each and moves on.
items.pourquoi_faux: The reasons are stated but not explained or supported. This is a list, not an argument.
items.correction_markdown: Develop each reason with an explanation and an example, using point, explanation, example.

items.erreur_markdown: The student tells a story about a day at school instead of giving arguments.
items.pourquoi_faux: A narrative is a different type of composition. An argumentative essay must persuade the reader.
items.correction_markdown: Use arguments and examples. A short real example is fine, but it must support a reason.

items.erreur_markdown: The conclusion introduces a completely new argument, or simply copies the introduction word for word.
items.pourquoi_faux: A conclusion closes the essay. New arguments cannot be developed, and repetition adds nothing.
items.correction_markdown: Restate your position in different words, summarise the main reasons and end with a final thought.

items.erreur_markdown: The essay uses text-message English such as "u" for "you" and "gonna" for "going to".
items.pourquoi_faux: Examiners expect formal written English. These forms are wrong in an essay and lose marks for expression and accuracy.
items.correction_markdown: Write full words and formal sentences: "you" and "going to".

items.enonce_markdown:
Write a one-sentence thesis statement in answer to this question, with two reasons.

"Pupils should wear school uniform. Do you agree?"
items.solution_markdown: Award marks for a clear position and two distinct reasons in one grammatical sentence. A model answer: **I agree that pupils should wear school uniform because it treats all pupils equally and makes them easy to recognise.** A disagreeing thesis is equally acceptable if it gives two reasons.

items.enonce_markdown:
Write the introduction (three or four sentences) of an essay on this question.

"Students should spend part of their weekend doing community work. Do you agree?"
items.solution_markdown: Award marks for brief background, a clear thesis and a hint of the reasons to come, with no argument developed yet. A model answer: **Many communities in Cameroon depend on the work of volunteers to keep their roads and markets clean. Some people believe that students should give part of their weekend to such work. I agree, because it teaches responsibility, it benefits the community and it prepares students for adult life.**

items.enonce_markdown:
Prepare an argumentative essay on this question.

"Television does more good than harm to children. Do you agree?"

(a) Write a plan with a thesis, two reasons, an opposing view and your reply.
(b) Write one fully developed body paragraph.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Award marks for each part. A model plan: thesis, television does more good than harm; reason 1, it educates through news and school programmes; reason 2, it entertains and helps families to relax together; opposing view, children may watch too much and neglect homework; reply, parents can set limits, so the harm is avoidable.

(b) A model paragraph: **First, television educates children. Programmes about science, history and health explain ideas in a lively way, so a child may understand a lesson better after seeing it on the screen. For example, a pupil who sees a programme about rivers may remember more in the next geography lesson. Education is therefore one of the greatest benefits of television.** Award marks for the topic sentence, the explanation, the example and the link back to the thesis.

items_markdown: An argumentative essay answers "Do you agree?" with a clear position kept from the introduction to the conclusion.
Plan before you write: thesis, two or three reasons with examples, one opposing view and your reply.
Develop every paragraph with point, explanation, example. A bare list of reasons is not an argument.
Use linking words to show addition, reason, result, contrast and conclusion.
Write formal, accurate English. The conclusion restates your position and brings no new argument.
